blocks.text: [III, 189] That is, a serpent is said to prick with its bite, because it has very sharp teeth. Varro in Priscian: When the asp, brought near, has pricked. Accordingly, the bite of the chersydrus and of the dragon is called νύγμα [nygma] in Nicander's Theriaca, that is, a pricking, at lines 362 and 446; just as in Aelian's History, book 15, chapter 13, the haemorrhous by its bite νύγμα ἐργάζεται [nygma ergazetai], produces a puncture, etc. And the three Arabic verbs لدغ [ladagha] ladaga, لسع [lasaʿa] lasaa, and وكع [wakaʿa] vvachaa, although they properly mean to prick and are often used of the scorpion, nevertheless also apply to the bite of a serpent, because it is a kind of pricking.

The second passage, Es. XI, 8. The infant shall delight itself over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child puts his hand upon the den of the basilisk, we have already explained earlier ^{b)} in the chapter On the Asp. Here, therefore, note only that the den of the basilisk is called in Hebrew מאורת צפעוני, and that the word מאורת occurs nowhere else for den. That is why translators struggle with rendering it. The more recent ones, with Jerome, render it den; but the Greeks have κοίτην [koitēn], as the Arabic has مضجع [maḍjaʿ], lair, as if they had read מעונת meonath instead of מאורת meürath, which they render κοίτην [koitēn] in Iob. XXXVII, 8. and XXXVIII, 40. and Ierem. X, 22. For the Chaldee, again, מאורת is something quite different, namely the pupil of the eye, as if from the root אור, which means to be bright or to be illuminated. Hence arose that paraphrase, על חיור גלגלי עיני חיוי חרמן חסילא ידוהי יושיט, Upon the sight (that is, the surface) of the pupil of the eye of the basilisk the weaned child shall put his hand. Hence Aben-Ezra: מאורת העין שהיא בעלת האור, Meürath, the eye, because it is endowed with light. That is, as Kimchi has it here: when the serpent is in its hole, and in that dark place the pupil of its eye shines, the child, seeing the light from outside and thinking it a precious stone or crystal, stretches out his hand to take it. So he, following the mind of the Chaldee translator. But the same author, in his own view, holds that מאורת, den, is named from אור, or light, which it admits through its opening; just as in Iud. VI, 2. the Israelites are said, out of fear of the Midianites, to have made for themselves in the mountains את המנהרות, that is, caves, so called because of the window through which נהרה, light, enters. In Selomoh, R. Menachem compares it with the word אור ur, which they explain as valley in Gen. XI, 28. and Es. XXIV, 15. I compare it with the Arabic أار [aʾār] aar, which the Arabs, in Giggeius, interpret as cave. For our Golius teaches that آر [ār] is to be referred to the root أور [ʾawr]. Thus آر [ār] and מאורה are words of the same origin, however different their form ^{(4)}.
